questions.question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select 'No improvement'.

The name, Khajuraho, has probably __been derived from__ the word 'Khajoor', meaning date palm.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '4' i.e. No improvement .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence states that the name "Khajuraho" has "probably been derived" from the word "Khajoor," meaning date palm. The phrase "has probably been derived" is grammatically correct and appropriately conveys the intended meaning.
 
• The verb "derived" is used correctly in the passive form, as it suggests that the name "Khajuraho" originated from the word "Khajoor."
 
• None of the alternative options, such as "be derived into," "derive at," or "derives into," are suitable in this context. They either do not fit the grammatical structure or fail to convey the intended meaning.

Correct sentence: *The name, Khajuraho, has probably been derived from the word 'Khajoor,' meaning date palm.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The passive form of a verb is used when the subject is the recipient of the action rather than the doer of the action.
 
• The phrase "has probably been derived" is in the present perfect passive tense, which is used to describe an action that has a connection to the present.
 
• Examples of correct usage:
 
 
• The recipe has been passed down through generations.
 
• The story has been adapted from a famous novel.

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options. If you don't find any error, mark 'No error' as your answer.

You have spoilt / the little chance you / had at succeeding.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '4' i.e. No error .

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence "You have spoilt the little chance you had at succeeding" is grammatically correct and free of any errors.
 
• "Spoilt" is the past participle of "spoil," and though "spoiled" is more common in American English, "spoilt" is widely accepted in British English.
 
• The phrase "the little chance you had at succeeding" correctly uses the noun phrase and relative clause without any error.
 
• The sentence meaningfully expresses that the small opportunity one had to succeed has been ruined or wasted.

Correct sentence: *You have spoilt the little chance you had at succeeding.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **British vs. American English:** "Spoilt" is used predominantly in British English, while "spoiled" is the preferred form in American English.
 
• **Past participle forms:** Both forms are grammatically correct; usage depends on the variant of English and context.
 
• **Common error checking:** Always consider the variety of English in use when evaluating words like "spoilt" vs. "spoiled."

options.text: I went to watch a play with one of my friends.

__
 
• The sentence "**He resides near an university**" contains a grammatical error regarding the use of the article **'an'**.
 
• The article **'an'** is used before words that begin with a vowel sound. However, the word "**university**" begins with a consonant sound **/juː/** (as in 'you'), not a vowel sound.
 
• Hence, the correct article to use in this context is **'a'**, not **'an'**.

• **Rules for using 'a' and 'an':**
 
 
• Use **'a'** before words that begin with a consonant sound (e.g., a cat, a dog, a university).
 
• Use **'an'** before words that begin with a vowel sound (e.g., an apple, an orange, an hour).
 
 
 
• **Note:** The choice of **'a' or 'an'** depends on the sound of the word, not the letter it starts with. For example:
 
 
• 'An hour' (silent 'h', vowel sound).
 
• 'A house' (pronounced 'h', consonant sound).

questions.question:
Select the appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed word in the following sentence to make it grammatically correct.

The grapes taste __(__sweetest__).__.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**sweet**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• The verb "**taste**" in this sentence is a linking verb. Linking verbs connect the subject to a word or phrase that describes or identifies the subject.
 
• When a linking verb is used, it should be followed by an adjective that describes the subject, not an adverb. The adjective tells us about the state or quality of the subject (the grapes).
 
• "**Sweet**" is an adjective in its positive degree.
 
• "**Sweetest**" is the superlative degree of the adjective, used when comparing three or more things. The sentence is not making a comparison, nor is it implying that these grapes are the sweetest among all grapes. It's simply describing their taste.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 3**.

 

Complete Sentence: *"The grapes taste sweet__."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** 

 
• **Option 1: "more sweeter"** – This is grammatically incorrect. "Sweeter" is already the comparative form; adding "more" makes it a double comparative.
 
• **Option 2: "sweeter"** – This is the comparative degree, used when comparing two things (e.g., "These grapes taste sweeter than those"). The original sentence doesn't imply a comparison.
 
• **Option 4: "most sweeter"** – This is also grammatically incorrect, being a double comparative with the superlative form.
